items.title: Labarbera interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2021
items.q: I played trumpet on Buddy’s band for about four months.

ctx.x: How do you — what was your entrance like into that world? © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

Well Buddy Rich of course put me on the map. You know I played trumpet on Buddy’s band for about four months. He fired me a couple of times, at least a couple of times. But I learned a lot on that band. Of course playing in bands, like with my parents with our family band, you understand how things work. You hear the melody then you hear the counter line. And when I was playing in college, when I played in big bands in college, I had my own big band in Potsdam. Well you get to hear all those inner voicings and…
Well I wondered how you, like if there was a real door that opened you, for your composing and I think you said Buddy Rich because you came back and started writing for him, is that correct?

items.title: Labarbera interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2021
items.q: I had almost done seven years with Buddy Rich of doing the other thing.

ctx.x: Nice. Well I’ll read what they said. They should have called you. In regards to your style, “His style is derived principally from that of John Coltrane to which he adds his own rhythmic looseness and lyricism.

Yeah I mean you listen to early Trane and it’s Prez and it’s Gene Ammons and it’s Dexter you know. I mean they’re all in there. I mean everybody’s kind of mixed up in there. But I mean the time that I was probably being more recognized for my soloing would have been with Elvin Jones. With Buddy of course I was known as a soloist but with a big band you’re only going to get a small chunk of space to solo. Right? Maybe one big feature that you get that you know — the suite was something that I kind of inherited…
Can you describe what that was like? Leaving the club after seeing Coltrane?
